questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.1 Applicability of Part 107 and key definitions
questions.text: A manufacturer is assessing whether its new aircraft falls under 14 CFR Part 107. The finished aircraft weighs 54.9 pounds including all installed components and payload at the time of operation. Under Part 107, does this aircraft qualify as a small unmanned aircraft?

answers.text: Yes, because it weighs less than 55 pounds including payload, meeting the Part 107 definition
No, because any aircraft exceeding 50 pounds must be operated under Part 61 regulations
Yes, but only after the payload is detached; Part 107 weight is calculated without attached accessories
No, because Part 107 applies only to aircraft weighing 0.55 pounds or less

explanations.a: 14 CFR 107.1 defines a small unmanned aircraft as one weighing less than 55 pounds, including payload, at the time of the flight, so 54.9 pounds qualifies.
explanations.b: Part 61 governs manned pilot certification and sets no 50-pound sUAS threshold; Part 107 sets the limit at less than 55 pounds.
explanations.c: The weight includes everything onboard during the operation including payload; removing payload to reclassify the aircraft misapplies the regulation.
explanations.d: The 0.55-pound figure is the registration threshold under Part 48, not the Part 107 applicability limit, which is less than 55 pounds.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.1 Applicability of Part 107 and key definitions
questions.text: During ground school, an instructor asks students which components together constitute a small unmanned aircraft system (sUAS) as defined in 14 CFR Part 107. The definition is important because all enumerated elements are subject to Part 107 requirements. Which answer correctly describes an sUAS?

answers.text: Only the unmanned aircraft itself along with its onboard battery and fuel source
The unmanned aircraft, its communication links, and all associated elements required for safe and efficient operation in the NAS
The unmanned aircraft, its dedicated ground support vehicle, and any radio spectrum licenses held by the operator
Only the ground control station software and the autopilot module used to program flight paths

explanations.a: The definition extends beyond the airframe and power source to include communication links and all other required associated elements.
explanations.b: 14 CFR 107.3 defines a small unmanned aircraft system as the small unmanned aircraft and its associated elements, including communication links and components required for safe and efficient NAS operation.
explanations.c: Ground vehicles and radio spectrum licenses are not enumerated components in the Part 107 sUAS definition.
explanations.d: The ground control station alone does not constitute the sUAS; both the aircraft and all associated elements together form the system.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.2 Falsification, accident reporting, inspection/compliance
questions.text: An FAA investigation reveals that a remote pilot altered a maintenance record to show a propeller inspection was completed when it was not. Under 14 CFR Part 107, which consequence represents the maximum regulatory penalty for this type of falsification?

answers.text: A 90-day suspension of the remote pilot certificate with mandatory remedial training
A civil penalty not to exceed $25,000 combined with a 180-day certificate suspension
Revocation of any airman certificate or rating held by the individual
A formal written warning entered into the FAA enforcement records database

explanations.a: A 90-day suspension is not the maximum; falsification is among the most serious violations and can result in the more severe outcome of certificate revocation.
explanations.b: While civil penalties can accompany enforcement actions, the specific statutory maximum for falsification under Part 107 is certificate revocation, not a fixed-dollar penalty combined with suspension.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.7, falsification, reproduction, or alteration of any certificate, rating, authorization, record, or report is grounds for revocation of any airman certificate or rating held.
explanations.d: A written warning is the mildest enforcement action and is not the maximum penalty; falsification is treated as a serious offense warranting certificate action.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.2 Falsification, accident reporting, inspection/compliance
questions.text: During an aerial inspection, a remote pilot loses control of their sUAS and it strikes a parked commercial vehicle, causing $650 in damage. No persons are injured and the sUAS is destroyed. Under 14 CFR Part 107, within how many calendar days must the remote PIC report this accident to the FAA?

answers.text: 2 calendar days from the date of the accident
5 calendar days from the date of the accident
7 calendar days from the date of the accident
10 calendar days from the date of the accident

explanations.a: 2 calendar days is not the Part 107 accident reporting window; the regulation specifies a 10-calendar-day deadline.
explanations.b: 5 calendar days does not match the Part 107 requirement; the deadline is 10 calendar days from the date of the accident.
explanations.c: 7 calendar days is not the correct deadline; 14 CFR 107.9 sets the reporting period at 10 calendar days.
explanations.d: 14 CFR 107.9 requires the remote PIC to report to the FAA within 10 calendar days when an accident results in serious injury, loss of consciousness, or property damage exceeding $500 other than to the sUAS itself.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.3 Multiple-category sUAS, record retention, previously manufactured sUAS
questions.text: A remote pilot owns a consumer-grade drone produced before 14 CFR Part 89 Remote ID compliance dates took effect, making it a previously manufactured sUAS. This aircraft lacks built-in Remote ID broadcast capability. Under Part 89, where is this aircraft legally permitted to fly?

answers.text: Anywhere in Class G airspace at or below 400 ft AGL without restriction
Only within a designated FAA-Recognized Identification Area (FRIA)
Within a 5-mile radius of the operator's declared primary operating location
In any airspace, provided the operator carries documentation proving the aircraft's manufacture date

explanations.a: Previously manufactured sUAS lacking compliant Remote ID are not freely permitted in Class G airspace; they are limited to FAA-Recognized Identification Areas.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR Part 89, sUAS without Remote ID capability, including previously manufactured UAS, may only operate within FAA-Recognized Identification Areas (FRIAs) where Remote ID is not required.
explanations.c: Proximity to the operator's declared location is not a recognized Remote ID exception in the regulations.
explanations.d: Carrying manufacture date documentation does not create a blanket Remote ID exemption; only FRIA operations satisfy this exception.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.3 Multiple-category sUAS, record retention, previously manufactured sUAS
questions.text: An sUAS has been declared by its manufacturer to satisfy requirements for both Category 1 and Category 2 under Part 107 Operations Over People rules. A remote pilot intends to fly it over an outdoor concert crowd. Which statement accurately describes how the multiple-category sUAS concept works?

answers.text: The aircraft must carry a separate registration number for each applicable operations category before flying over people
Both categories apply simultaneously, requiring the pilot to satisfy the stricter of the two category-specific requirement sets
The remote pilot may choose to operate under any category the aircraft satisfies, meeting only that chosen category's requirements
The manufacturer must submit one unified Declaration of Compliance covering all qualifying categories before any over-people flight

explanations.a: Registration does not need to be duplicated per category; a single Part 48 registration covers the aircraft regardless of operational category chosen.
explanations.b: There is no requirement to satisfy the stricter of two categories simultaneously; the remote pilot selects one qualifying category per operation.
explanations.c: Part 107 allows an sUAS that meets requirements of more than one category to be flown under whichever qualifying category the remote pilot selects, provided all of that category's requirements are satisfied.
explanations.d: Declarations of Compliance are category-specific; there is no unified multi-category document requirement, and the remote pilot selects the applicable category per operation.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.4 Registration (Parts 47/48)
questions.text: A hobbyist assembles a custom sUAS from commercially available parts. The completed aircraft weighs exactly 0.60 pounds with all installed components. The hobbyist plans to fly it recreationally at a public park. Under 14 CFR Part 48, what registration requirement applies?

answers.text: Registration is not required because the aircraft is home-assembled and qualifies for the builder's exemption
Registration applies only if the aircraft will be flown for compensation or other commercial purposes
Registration is triggered only when operating within 5 miles of a public-use airport
Registration is required because the aircraft meets or exceeds 0.55 pounds and must be registered before any outdoor flight

explanations.a: There is no home-assembly registration exemption under Part 48; any sUAS weighing 0.55 pounds or more must be registered regardless of how it was built.
explanations.b: Part 48 registration applies to both recreational and commercial operations and is not limited to flights for compensation.
explanations.c: Proximity to an airport does not determine registration requirements; the 0.55-pound weight threshold triggers the registration obligation.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR Part 48, any unmanned aircraft weighing 0.55 pounds (250 grams) or more must be registered with the FAA before operating outdoors, whether for recreational or commercial use.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.4 Registration (Parts 47/48)
questions.text: After registering an sUAS under 14 CFR Part 48, a remote pilot receives a Certificate of Aircraft Registration and wants to know when renewal is required. According to Part 48, this registration certificate is valid for how long?

answers.text: 3 years from the date the Certificate of Aircraft Registration is issued
2 years, aligning with the 24-month aeronautical knowledge recurrency cycle under Part 107
5 years from the date of initial Part 48 registration
Indefinitely, as long as the aircraft remains in the same owner's continuous possession

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR Part 48, a Certificate of Aircraft Registration for an sUAS is valid for 3 years from the date it is issued, after which it must be renewed.
explanations.b: The 2-year period corresponds to the aeronautical knowledge recurrency requirement under Part 107, not the Part 48 registration validity period.
explanations.c: 5 years is not the correct validity period; Part 48 establishes a 3-year registration cycle.
explanations.d: sUAS registration does expire and must be renewed every 3 years; it does not remain valid indefinitely based on continuous ownership.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.5 Condition for safe operation and medical conditions
questions.text: A remote pilot woke up with a significant headache and mild vertigo on the morning of a scheduled commercial sUAS operation. No Aviation Medical Examiner is available before the flight. Under 14 CFR Part 107, who is responsible for determining whether the pilot is fit to act as remote PIC?

answers.text: The FAA Flight Standards District Office, which must be notified of any potential medical concern before commercial flights
An Aviation Medical Examiner who must issue a current third-class medical certificate before any commercial sUAS flight
The remote pilot themselves, who must self-assess fitness and ground themselves if a condition would interfere with safe operations
The operator's designated safety officer, who completes a pre-flight wellness check on all commercial remote pilots

explanations.a: The FSDO is not involved in pre-flight fitness determinations; Part 107 does not require FSDO notification for individual pilot medical concerns.
explanations.b: Part 107 does not require any class of FAA medical certificate; there is no AME involvement in routine sUAS fitness assessments.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.17, the remote pilot must not operate the sUAS if they know or have reason to know that a physical or mental condition would interfere with safe operation; this is a self-assessment responsibility.
explanations.d: Part 107 places the fitness determination solely on the remote pilot; there is no provision for a designated safety officer to make this determination on the pilot's behalf.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.5 Condition for safe operation and medical conditions
questions.text: A remote pilot takes a prescription sedative for a sleep disorder and has a scheduled sUAS operation the following morning. The medication was taken 6 hours before the planned flight time and the prescribing physician noted the drug causes drowsiness for up to 8 hours. Under Part 107, which course of action is correct?

answers.text: Proceed with the flight because prescription medications are permitted under Part 107 when a licensed physician authorized them
Proceed if a visual observer is positioned to maintain VLOS independently, reducing the impaired pilot's workload
Conduct only a brief hover test not to exceed 100 feet AGL to assess whether impairment is present before continuing
Ground the sUAS because the sedative's active drowsiness effect would likely interfere with safe operation

explanations.a: Having a valid prescription does not automatically permit operation; Part 107 prohibits flying when any physical or mental condition, including drug side effects, would interfere with safe operation.
explanations.b: A visual observer's presence does not eliminate the remote PIC's obligation to be fit to operate; the pilot remains responsible for safe conduct of the flight.
explanations.c: Conducting any flight while potentially impaired by medication violates Part 107; a short hover test does not resolve or excuse the underlying disqualifying condition.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 107.17, a remote pilot must not operate an sUAS if they know or have reason to know that a physical or mental condition would interfere with safe operation; an active sedative causing drowsiness qualifies as such a condition.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.6 Remote PIC responsibility, manipulating controls, in-flight emergency deviation
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to let a college student with no FAA certification manipulate the flight controls of a small quadcopter during a supervised training session. Under 14 CFR Part 107, may the remote PIC allow the student to manipulate the controls?

answers.text: Yes, provided the remote PIC is able to immediately take over direct control of the sUAS if needed and remains the acting PIC throughout
Yes, but only if the student holds at least a student remote pilot certificate issued by the FAA
No, manipulating flight controls is restricted exclusively to individuals who hold a current remote pilot certificate
No, sUAS control may never be shared with a second person under any Part 107 circumstances

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.12, a remote PIC may allow another person to manipulate the flight controls as long as the remote PIC can immediately take direct control if needed; no certificate is required for the person assisting.
explanations.b: Part 107 does not require the assisting person to hold a student or any other remote pilot certificate; only the remote PIC must be certificated.
explanations.c: There is no Part 107 restriction limiting flight control manipulation to certificate holders; the key requirement is that the remote PIC retains override authority.
explanations.d: Part 107 explicitly allows another person to manipulate the flight controls under the remote PIC's active supervision.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.6 Remote PIC responsibility, manipulating controls, in-flight emergency deviation
questions.text: While conducting a film operation, a remote PIC experiences sudden interference that causes the aircraft to drift beyond VLOS, prompting an emergency landing in the safest available clearing to prevent injury. No injuries or third-party property damage result. What is the remote PIC's reporting obligation under Part 107?

answers.text: File a NOTAM describing the emergency within 24 hours and notify the local FSDO by telephone the same day
Submit a written report to the FAA upon request if the FAA asks for an explanation of the deviation from Part 107 rules
Immediately contact the nearest ATC facility by radio to report the in-flight emergency before resuming any operations
Complete an NTSB Form 6120.1 and submit it within 5 days regardless of whether the FAA requests a report

explanations.a: There is no NOTAM filing or mandatory proactive FSDO notification requirement for in-flight emergency deviations under Part 107.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.21, in an in-flight emergency the remote PIC may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary and, if requested by the FAA, must submit a written report explaining the deviation.
explanations.c: Part 107 does not require radio communication with ATC following an emergency deviation; the obligation is a written report to the FAA only upon FAA request.
explanations.d: NTSB Form 6120.1 is for accidents meeting specific injury or damage thresholds; a control link deviation without injury or qualifying damage does not trigger NTSB reporting, and the Part 107 report is only required upon FAA request.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.7 Hazardous operations, alcohol/drugs
questions.text: A remote pilot is hired to drop promotional paper flyers from an sUAS over a busy outdoor market containing hundreds of shoppers. The flyers are lightweight single-page sheets. Under 14 CFR Part 107, which statement about this object drop is correct?

answers.text: Dropping lightweight paper materials is fully permitted because they pose no structural hazard to persons below
Dropping any object from an sUAS is categorically prohibited under all circumstances in Part 107
Dropping materials is permitted as long as the sUAS stays above 400 ft AGL during the entire drop sequence
Dropping an object is prohibited if it creates a hazard to persons or property on the surface, regardless of object weight

explanations.a: Paper flyers can still create hazards over crowds, and low weight alone does not determine legality; the risk to persons below is the determining standard.
explanations.b: Part 107 does not categorically ban all object drops; the prohibition applies when dropping the object endangers persons or property.
explanations.c: Altitude alone does not make an object drop safe or legal; the test is whether the action endangers persons or property on the surface.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 107.23(b), no person may operate an sUAS to drop an object if doing so creates a hazard to persons or property on the surface; over a dense outdoor market, a flyer drop would likely endanger persons below.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.7 Hazardous operations, alcohol/drugs
questions.text: A real estate company wants its remote pilot to launch an sUAS from a slowly moving golf cart while photographing a suburban neighborhood for marketing purposes. Under 14 CFR Part 107, operating an sUAS from a moving ground vehicle is permitted only when which specific condition is met?

answers.text: The operation takes place over a sparsely populated area and is not conducted from a moving aircraft
The vehicle travels at no more than 15 mph and the remote pilot holds a valid state driver's license
The remote pilot maintains VLOS of the aircraft and files a NOTAM at least 30 minutes in advance
An FAA certificate of waiver for moving-vehicle operations has been approved under Part 107 Subpart D

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.25, operating from a moving land or water-borne vehicle is permitted when conducted over a sparsely populated area; operating from a moving aircraft is never allowed.
explanations.b: Vehicle speed limits and driver's license possession are not the regulatory conditions; the sparsely populated area criterion is what governs moving-vehicle launches.
explanations.c: VLOS maintenance is always required independently, but it is not the specific enabling condition for moving-vehicle launches; the sparsely populated area requirement controls.
explanations.d: No waiver is required for moving land-vehicle operations in sparsely populated areas; Part 107.25 permits this without a waiver.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.8 Daylight, civil twilight, and night operations
questions.text: A remote pilot plans a real estate photography flight beginning 20 minutes before official sunrise, which falls within Part 107's civil twilight window. Beyond all standard Part 107 operating requirements, what specific equipment must the sUAS have for this civil twilight operation?

answers.text: Navigation lights showing red on the left and green on the right, matching manned aircraft Part 91 equipment standards
Anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles under the prevailing conditions
A ground crew marker light directed at the aircraft from the launch point throughout the flight
A forward-facing thermal imaging sensor capable of detecting flight obstacles in low-light conditions

explanations.a: Part 107 does not require navigation lights; the specific lighting mandate for civil twilight and night operations is anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.29, sUAS operated during civil twilight or at night must have anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles.
explanations.c: A ground crew marker light is not a Part 107 requirement; the regulation specifies anti-collision lighting mounted on and visible from the aircraft itself.
explanations.d: Thermal imaging sensors address payload capabilities, not the lighting safety requirement mandated by 107.29 for civil twilight operations.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.8 Daylight, civil twilight, and night operations
questions.text: A remote pilot in the continental United States wants to launch as early as possible under Part 107's civil twilight provision without obtaining a waiver. The published official sunrise at the operation's location is 06:15. Civil twilight operations under Part 107 are authorized beginning at what local time?

answers.text: 05:30, which is 45 minutes before the published official sunrise
06:00, which is 15 minutes before the published official sunrise
05:45, which is 30 minutes before the published official sunrise
06:15 exactly, because any flight before official sunrise always requires a waiver under Part 107

explanations.a: 45 minutes before sunrise extends beyond the civil twilight window; Part 107 sets the authorized boundary at 30 minutes before official sunrise.
explanations.b: 15 minutes before sunrise falls within civil twilight but is not the beginning of the authorized window; the window opens 30 minutes before official sunrise.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.29 and the definition in 107.3, civil twilight is the period from 30 minutes before official sunrise to 30 minutes after official sunset, making 05:45 (06:15 minus 30 minutes) the earliest authorized launch time.
explanations.d: Flight before official sunrise during civil twilight does not require a waiver, provided the required anti-collision lighting is equipped; a waiver is not necessary for civil twilight operations.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.9 VLOS and visual observer requirements
questions.text: Part 107 requires the remote PIC or visual observer to maintain visual line of sight (VLOS) of the sUAS at all times. A remote pilot who wears prescription eyeglasses wants to confirm compliance with the VLOS standard. According to 14 CFR Part 107, VLOS must be maintained using what type of vision?

answers.text: Unaided vision only, requiring removal of all corrective eyewear including prescription glasses during sUAS operations
Vision aided by a first-person view camera system that the FAA has approved for VLOS purposes
Unaided vision, with the specific exception that ordinary corrective lenses such as glasses or contact lenses are permitted
Any vision assistance technology including FPV displays, binoculars, or telescopic lenses, all of which qualify under VLOS

explanations.a: Corrective lenses are explicitly permitted under Part 107; requiring their removal would be unsafe and contrary to the regulation.
explanations.b: FPV camera systems do not satisfy the VLOS requirement; the regulation requires direct unaided visual contact with the aircraft.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.31, VLOS means the remote PIC and any visual observer must be able to see the unmanned aircraft with vision unaided by any device other than corrective lenses such as glasses or contacts.
explanations.d: Binoculars, telescopic lenses, and FPV displays are explicitly excluded from the VLOS standard; only corrective lenses are permitted as an exception.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.9 VLOS and visual observer requirements
questions.text: A remote pilot uses a visual observer (VO) to extend situational awareness during a complex mapping operation, with both positioned at different points around the flight area. Under 14 CFR Part 107, which statement correctly describes what a visual observer must do?

answers.text: The visual observer must hold a current Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate to legally serve in that role
The visual observer may use binoculars to extend effective line-of-sight range over larger operational areas
The visual observer may divide attention between two sUAS simultaneously if each aircraft has a separate remote PIC
The visual observer must maintain VLOS of the sUAS and communicate observed hazards or VLOS loss to the remote PIC

explanations.a: Part 107 does not require a visual observer to hold a remote pilot certificate; the VO's role is practical, not certificate-based.
explanations.b: Binoculars and other magnifying devices do not satisfy the VLOS standard and may not be used by a VO to extend effective viewing range.
explanations.c: A visual observer may not divide attention among multiple aircraft; each VO is associated with a single flight and a single aircraft.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 107.33, a visual observer must maintain VLOS of the unmanned aircraft and communicate to the remote PIC any hazard or loss of VLOS observed during the operation.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.10 Multiple sUAS prohibition, hazmat prohibition
questions.text: An experienced operator proposes to simultaneously control three separate sUAS during a large outdoor event, each on its own radio frequency and each monitored by a dedicated visual observer. Under 14 CFR Part 107, is this arrangement permitted?

answers.text: No, a single remote PIC may operate only one sUAS at a time regardless of how many visual observers or radio frequencies are used
Yes, because each aircraft has a dedicated visual observer and the rule only limits unassisted simultaneous control
Yes, for commercial large-event operations because the FAA recognizes multi-aircraft fleet exceptions for professional operators
No, but only if any individual aircraft weighs more than 2 pounds; lighter aircraft may be flown simultaneously under one PIC

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.35, no person may act as remote PIC of more than one sUAS at the same time; the presence of visual observers and separate frequencies does not change this requirement.
explanations.b: The visual observer provision addresses VLOS extension, not the prohibition on simultaneous PIC duties; one PIC may not serve multiple aircraft at once.
explanations.c: There is no large-event commercial exception in Part 107 permitting one remote PIC to operate multiple sUAS simultaneously.
explanations.d: The prohibition on simultaneous multiple sUAS operations applies regardless of individual aircraft weight; there is no weight-based exception in 107.35.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.10 Multiple sUAS prohibition, hazmat prohibition
questions.text: A research company wants to use a 6-pound sUAS to transport a 1.5-pound sealed canister of liquid nitrogen (a cryogenic hazardous material) between two campus lab buildings. The total aircraft weight remains well under 55 pounds. Under Part 107, is this transport operation permitted?

answers.text: Yes, because the total weight stays under the 55-pound Part 107 limit and the cryogenic material is sealed in its canister
No, because Part 107 prohibits transporting hazardous materials on a small unmanned aircraft without exception
Yes, provided the remote pilot files a hazardous material transport declaration with the FAA at least 48 hours before the flight
Yes, if the operation is restricted to below 200 ft AGL and conducted exclusively over uninhabited campus grounds

explanations.a: Weight compliance does not override the hazardous material prohibition; Part 107 bans hazmat carriage regardless of aircraft total weight or payload containment.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.36, no person may carry hazardous material on a small unmanned aircraft; liquid nitrogen is a DOT hazardous material, and no waiver or declaration process exists to permit hazmat transport under Part 107.
explanations.c: Part 107 contains no hazardous material declaration filing procedure that would authorize such transport; the prohibition is absolute within Part 107 operations.
explanations.d: Altitude and area restrictions do not create an exception to the hazardous material prohibition; the ban applies regardless of operational parameters.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.11 Right-of-way, see-and-avoid
questions.keyword: manned aircraft unconditional right of way
questions.text: A remote pilot is operating an sUAS at 300 ft AGL when a small Cessna approaches the same area at approximately the same altitude on a converging course. Under 14 CFR Part 107, which aircraft has the right of way?

answers.text: The sUAS, because smaller and lighter aircraft are more vulnerable to collision damage
The manned Cessna, because the sUAS must always yield the right of way to all manned aircraft
The faster aircraft, since the slower aircraft has more time available to execute a maneuver
The aircraft at lower altitude, because lower aircraft have priority at converging altitude levels

explanations.a: Size and vulnerability do not determine right of way under Part 107; the rule requires the sUAS to yield to manned aircraft unconditionally.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.37, the remote PIC must yield the right of way to all manned aircraft; the Cessna as a manned aircraft always has right of way over the sUAS.
explanations.c: Relative speed is not a right-of-way criterion in Part 107; the sUAS must yield to manned aircraft regardless of which aircraft is moving faster.
explanations.d: Altitude priority is not the applicable standard; Part 107 requires unconditional right-of-way deference to all manned aircraft.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.11 Right-of-way, see-and-avoid
questions.keyword: immediate evasive action head-on manned aircraft
questions.text: During an sUAS operation at 350 ft AGL, a remote pilot spots a helicopter approaching from the east at the same altitude on a direct head-on converging path. The pilot estimates about 15 seconds before the two aircraft reach the same point. What is the correct immediate action under Part 107?

answers.text: Immediately maneuver the sUAS away from the helicopter's path to yield right of way and ensure separation
Hold current altitude and course because head-on encounters require the approaching helicopter to deviate to its right
Descend the sUAS to hover stationary, allowing the helicopter pilot to maneuver around the stopped aircraft
Attempt radio contact with the helicopter on CTAF before taking any evasive maneuver to coordinate an avoidance plan

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.37, the remote PIC must yield right of way to all manned aircraft; immediate evasive maneuvering of the sUAS to create separation from the helicopter is required.
explanations.b: Head-on right-of-way conventions for two manned aircraft do not apply to the sUAS; Part 107 requires the sUAS to yield unconditionally to any manned aircraft.
explanations.c: Hovering in place does not satisfy the right-of-way yield requirement; the sUAS must actively maneuver away from the approaching manned aircraft.
explanations.d: Radio contact is not required before taking evasive action, and the 15-second window requires immediate response; most sUAS have no radio communication capability anyway.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.12 Airspace authorization, operations near airports, prohibited/restricted areas, NOTAM-based TFRs
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to fly at 200 ft AGL in an area that falls within Class D airspace surrounding a regional airport. The pilot holds a Part 107 certificate but has obtained no prior approval. Under Part 107, what must the pilot obtain before operating in this airspace?

answers.text: A NOTAM issued by FAA Flight Service authorizing the specific altitude and duration of the sUAS flight
A signed letter from the airport manager approving sUAS operations in proximity to the airport
Written authorization from the local FSDO submitted at least 72 hours before the intended flight
ATC authorization from the controlling facility or through an FAA-approved system such as LAANC or DroneZone

explanations.a: NOTAMs notify airspace users of hazards and conditions; they do not function as authorization documents for sUAS operations in controlled airspace.
explanations.b: Airport manager approval is not the regulatory authorization mechanism for operating in Class D airspace under Part 107.
explanations.c: FSDO written authorization is not the airspace access mechanism under Part 107; the FAA uses LAANC and the DroneZone portal for this purpose.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 107.41, no person may operate an sUAS in Class B, C, D, or surface Class E airspace without ATC authorization, obtainable through LAANC or the FAA DroneZone portal.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.12 Airspace authorization, operations near airports, prohibited/restricted areas, NOTAM-based TFRs
questions.text: A remote pilot launches an sUAS for a rooftop inspection while unaware that a TFR was established over the area one hour earlier. After 12 minutes of flight, the pilot notices the TFR listed in the NOTAMs they had not checked. Under Part 107, how is this situation classified?

answers.text: An excusable minor deviation, because the pilot had no actual knowledge of the TFR before launch
A voluntary disclosure situation eligible for the FAA Compliance Program with guaranteed immunity from enforcement
A violation of Part 107 that may result in civil penalties, certificate suspension, or certificate revocation
An automatic permanent disqualification from holding any remote pilot certificate under Part 107

explanations.a: Lack of actual knowledge of a TFR is not a legal defense; remote pilots are responsible for checking all applicable NOTAMs before each flight.
explanations.b: While voluntary disclosure through the FAA's Safety Assurance System may reduce penalties, it does not guarantee immunity, and the act itself remains a violation that may result in enforcement action.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.47 and the enforcement provisions at 107.57 and 107.59, operating in violation of a TFR is a Part 107 violation that may result in civil penalties, certificate suspension, or revocation.
explanations.d: There is no automatic permanent disqualification provision in Part 107 for TFR violations; the consequences are determined by enforcement action based on the specific circumstances.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.13 Preflight familiarization and inspection
questions.text: Before conducting an sUAS mapping flight over a large agricultural property, a remote PIC is subject to a preflight obligation imposed by Part 107. Which statement correctly describes the minimum preflight requirement under 14 CFR 107.49?

answers.text: File a flight plan with the nearest ATC facility listing the intended route, altitude, and estimated flight duration
Notify the local FSDO by telephone if the flight will last longer than 30 minutes or cross a county line
Perform only a battery voltage check to confirm the aircraft has adequate power for the intended mission
Familiarize yourself with all available information pertinent to the intended operation, including airspace, NOTAMs, weather, and aircraft performance data

explanations.a: Filing a flight plan with ATC is not required under Part 107; sUAS operations generally do not use the ATC flight plan system.
explanations.b: There is no FSDO notification requirement based on flight duration or geographic scope; the preflight obligation is broader in nature.
explanations.c: A battery check alone does not satisfy the preflight requirement; the regulation requires review of all pertinent available information before each flight.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 107.49, before each flight the remote PIC must familiarize themselves with all available information pertinent to the intended operation, encompassing airspace restrictions, NOTAMs, weather forecasts, aircraft performance, and local hazards.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.13 Preflight familiarization and inspection
questions.text: During a preflight inspection, a remote pilot finds a visible hairline crack in one of the landing gear arms. The aircraft is otherwise fully charged and the motors spin freely by hand. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what should the pilot do?

answers.text: Proceed with the flight if the crack does not extend to the motor mount and a brief hover test shows normal handling
Ground the sUAS and do not fly until the damage is properly assessed and the aircraft is confirmed in a condition for safe operation
Reduce payload weight by half and restrict the operation to below 100 ft AGL as a precautionary mitigation measure
Apply field tape over the crack, document it in the flight log, and proceed if the repair holds through a pre-takeoff vibration check

explanations.a: A short hover test does not confirm structural airworthiness; a visible crack is a defect that must be properly assessed before any flight.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.15, the remote PIC must ensure the sUAS is in a condition for safe operation before each flight; a visible structural crack must be assessed and resolved before the aircraft flies.
explanations.c: Reduced payload and altitude restrictions do not substitute for confirming the aircraft is structurally sound; the defect must first be addressed.
explanations.d: Field tape repairs and vibration checks do not constitute proper assessment of structural airworthiness; the aircraft must be repaired or inspected by a qualified person before flight.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.14 Operating limitations
questions.text: A client asks a remote pilot to fly their sUAS at maximum allowable speed to keep pace with a fast-moving subject vehicle during a commercial advertisement shoot. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what is the maximum groundspeed at which the remote pilot may legally operate the sUAS?

answers.text: 87 knots (100 miles per hour)
55 knots (63 miles per hour)
100 knots (115 miles per hour)
65 knots (75 miles per hour)

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.51(a), the maximum groundspeed for sUAS operations is 87 knots (100 miles per hour); this is the regulatory ceiling for standard Part 107 operations.
explanations.b: 55 knots is well below the Part 107 maximum; the regulation allows up to 87 knots groundspeed.
explanations.c: 100 knots exceeds the Part 107 groundspeed limit of 87 knots and is not authorized under standard Part 107 operations.
explanations.d: 65 knots is below the maximum authorized groundspeed of 87 knots established by 14 CFR 107.51.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.14 Operating limitations
questions.keyword: 400 ft AGL ceiling over open terrain
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to fly at 420 ft AGL over a flat, open agricultural field with no structures within 1 mile. No airspace authorization for higher altitudes has been obtained and no waiver is in effect. The pilot argues the view is better at that height. Under 14 CFR Part 107, is 420 ft AGL permitted here?

answers.text: Yes, because the 400-ft limit applies only within 5 miles of airports and not over open rural terrain
Yes, if a NOTAM is filed listing the higher altitude and the flight duration is under 30 minutes
No, because the 400-ft AGL ceiling applies over open terrain where no qualifying structure exception is available and no waiver exists
Yes, provided the pilot maintains continuous VLOS of the aircraft at that altitude throughout the flight

explanations.a: The 400-ft limit is not restricted to areas near airports; it applies to all Part 107 sUAS operations unless a specific regulatory exception applies.
explanations.b: Filing a NOTAM does not authorize flight above 400 ft AGL; a waiver or the structure exception is required to exceed this limit.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.51(b), sUAS may not exceed 400 ft AGL unless within 400 feet of a qualifying structure; over open farmland with no structures, 420 ft AGL exceeds the applicable limit.
explanations.d: Maintaining VLOS does not override altitude limitations; VLOS is a concurrent and independent requirement, not a substitute for altitude compliance.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.15 Automated operations, transportation of property
questions.text: A remote pilot programs an sUAS for a fully automated waypoint-following mission over a construction site. Once launched, the aircraft follows its preprogrammed path with no manual inputs. Under Part 107, who holds remote PIC responsibility during this automated flight?

answers.text: The remote pilot who initiated the mission retains PIC responsibility and must remain capable of intervening if needed
The software engineer who programmed the autonomous flight path assumes PIC liability for all automated flight segments
The property owner of the construction site who authorized the flight assumes legal responsibility once the aircraft is airborne
No PIC responsibility exists during automated flight; the aircraft is self-certifying under applicable FAA automation standards

explanations.a: Under Part 107, the remote PIC retains full responsibility for the safe conduct of every flight, including automated segments; the pilot must monitor the flight and be able to intervene as necessary.
explanations.b: Software developers are not recognized as remote PICs under Part 107; regulatory responsibility remains with the certificated remote pilot who initiated and oversees the operation.
explanations.c: Property ownership does not confer or transfer remote PIC responsibility; the certificated pilot launching and overseeing the mission holds PIC accountability.
explanations.d: Part 107 does not recognize a PIC-exempt category for automated operations; a certificated remote pilot must be responsible for the flight at all times.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.15 Automated operations, transportation of property
questions.text: A startup company wants to begin transporting small sealed packages between facilities using Part 107-certificated remote pilots. Regarding property transport under Part 107, which statement is most accurate?

answers.text: Only non-fragile goods weighing 5 pounds or less may be transported under standard Part 107 regulations
All commercial package delivery requires a separate Part 135 air carrier certificate and cannot be conducted under Part 107
Transporting property is addressed within Part 107, requiring that total weight stays under 55 pounds, the property does not create undue hazard, and all other Part 107 rules are met
Part 107 categorically forbids commercial delivery operations, requiring a separate FAA exemption for any package transport

explanations.a: Part 107 imposes no 5-pound payload restriction; the relevant constraint is that total aircraft weight including property must remain under 55 pounds.
explanations.b: While certain large-scale for-hire delivery operations may require Part 135 authority, property transport under Part 107 is addressed within Part 107 itself and is not categorically prohibited.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR Part 107 Subpart B, transporting property is permitted when the aircraft total weight including the property stays under 55 pounds, the property is secured to prevent shifting hazards, and all Part 107 operational rules are satisfied.
explanations.d: Part 107 does not categorically prohibit commercial package transport; compliance with all applicable rules, which may include Part 135 for certain operations, is required.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.16 ATC transponder and ADS-B Out prohibitions
questions.text: A remote pilot with an electronics background considers installing an ADS-B Out transmitter on their sUAS to allow ATC to track the drone and improve airspace safety. Under 14 CFR Part 107, the FAA prohibits ADS-B Out on sUAS primarily because of what specific concern?

answers.text: ADS-B Out signals from sUAS would interfere with ground-based primary and secondary radar systems used by ATC
Widespread sUAS transmission on ADS-B Out frequencies could degrade or disrupt the ADS-B system that manned aircraft rely on for traffic awareness in the NAS
ADS-B Out technology is reserved exclusively for fixed-wing aircraft operating under instrument flight rules and is incompatible with rotary sUAS
FAA ground ADS-B receiver stations cannot process position reports from aircraft operating below 400 ft AGL

explanations.a: ADS-B Out does not interfere with primary or secondary radar systems; the concern is the integrity of the ADS-B network itself used by manned aircraft.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.67, ADS-B Out is prohibited on sUAS because widespread sUAS use of ADS-B frequencies could degrade the ADS-B system that manned aircraft depend on for traffic situational awareness in the NAS.
explanations.c: ADS-B Out is used by various aircraft types including helicopters and turboprops; the prohibition is not about airframe configuration compatibility.
explanations.d: The prohibition is based on system integrity concerns for manned aviation, not on ADS-B receiver processing limitations at low altitudes.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.16 ATC transponder and ADS-B Out prohibitions
questions.text: An sUAS manufacturer builds a quadcopter with an integrated Mode C ATC transponder intended for safer airport proximity operations. A remote pilot purchases this aircraft and wants to activate the transponder while operating near a Class D airport to allow ATC to track the drone. Under 14 CFR Part 107, is operating with this transponder active permitted?

answers.text: Permitted in Class D airspace when the transponder is set to Mode C and squawking code 1200
Permitted after obtaining LAANC authorization, which validates the transponder use as part of the clearance
Permitted as a supplemental safety measure if all standard Part 107 authorization requirements are also met
Prohibited; 14 CFR 107.67 bans the operation of any sUAS equipped with ATC transponder equipment

explanations.a: Mode C squawk 1200 does not make transponder operation legal on an sUAS; the prohibition in Part 107 is categorical and not mode-dependent.
explanations.b: LAANC authorization addresses airspace access and does not authorize or validate transponder use; the prohibition is independent of airspace authorization.
explanations.c: No supplemental safety justification permits transponder use on sUAS under Part 107; the prohibition is unconditional within Part 107 operations.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 107.67, no person may operate a small unmanned aircraft with ATC transponder equipment; this prohibition protects transponder-based ATC services from interference.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.17 Remote Pilot Certificate eligibility and aeronautical knowledge recency
questions.text: A motivated 15-year-old wants to earn a Remote Pilot Certificate with an sUAS rating to conduct commercial drone photography for a local business. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what minimum age must an applicant meet to be eligible for this certificate?

answers.text: 14 years of age, which is also the minimum age to sit for the UAG certification knowledge test
17 years of age, aligning with the minimum age for a student pilot certificate under Part 61
16 years of age, as specified in the eligibility requirements of 14 CFR 107.61
18 years of age, because commercial sUAS operations require adult legal capacity under FAA regulations

explanations.a: 14 years is the minimum age to take the FAA UAG knowledge test per Appendix 1 of the ACS, but the minimum age to actually hold the Remote Pilot Certificate is 16 years.
explanations.b: 17 years is the minimum age for a student pilot certificate under Part 61; the remote pilot certificate minimum age under Part 107 is 16.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.61, an applicant for a Remote Pilot Certificate with an sUAS rating must be at least 16 years of age at the time of application.
explanations.d: There is no 18-year minimum for Part 107 commercial operations; the minimum certificate age is 16 years under 107.61.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.17 Remote Pilot Certificate eligibility and aeronautical knowledge recency
questions.text: A remote pilot passed the initial Part 107 UAG knowledge test two years ago and has been operating commercially since. Their 24-month aeronautical knowledge recurrency window expires this month. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what must the pilot complete to maintain knowledge currency?

answers.text: Log 25 hours of sUAS flight time in the preceding 12 months and submit a logbook to the FAA for verification
Meet with a Certificated Flight Instructor who reviews aeronautical knowledge and endorses the pilot's logbook
Obtain a current third-class FAA medical certificate demonstrating continued fitness to operate an sUAS
Complete the FAA's free online recurrent training course (ALC-677) within the preceding 24 calendar months; the recurrent knowledge test was eliminated effective August 2024

explanations.a: Submitting a Form 8710-13 every 24 months is not a recurrency requirement — the certificate itself does not expire; currency is maintained through the ALC-677 online course.
explanations.b: There is no requirement to log a specified number of operational flights for currency under Part 107; currency is satisfied solely by completing ALC-677 within the preceding 24 calendar months.
explanations.c: TSA vetting is part of initial certification, not recurrency. Currency under Part 107 is maintained by completing the FAA's free online ALC-677 recurrent training course every 24 calendar months.
explanations.d: Effective August 2024, the FAA replaced the recurrent UAG knowledge test with the free online ALC-677 recurrent training course. Remote pilots maintain currency by completing ALC-677 every 24 calendar months. The initial UAG knowledge test is still required for first-time certification, but recurrency no longer involves a knowledge test.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.18 Drug/alcohol offenses and refusal to test
questions.text: A remote pilot had their last alcoholic drink approximately 7 hours before a scheduled early-morning sUAS operation. The pilot feels alert and shows no obvious signs of impairment. Under 14 CFR Part 107 and the incorporated provisions of 14 CFR 91.17, may this pilot legally act as remote PIC?

answers.text: No, because the pilot consumed alcohol within the preceding 8 hours, which is prohibited regardless of perceived impairment level
Yes, because 7 hours of abstinence is generally sufficient and the pilot demonstrates no visible signs of impairment
Yes, as long as a visual observer is present to serve as an additional safety layer during the flight
No, but only if the flight is being conducted for compensation; recreational flights within 7 hours of alcohol consumption are permitted

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.27, which incorporates 91.17, no person may act as remote PIC within 8 hours of consuming alcohol; 7 hours falls within that prohibited window regardless of perceived sobriety.
explanations.b: Perceived alertness does not override the regulatory prohibition; the 8-hour rule is absolute and not subject to subjective impairment assessment by the pilot.
explanations.c: A visual observer's presence does not remove the remote PIC's legal disqualification from the 8-hour alcohol rule; the pilot is prohibited from acting as PIC.
explanations.d: The 8-hour alcohol prohibition applies equally to recreational and commercial sUAS operations; there is no compensation-based distinction in the rule.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.18 Drug/alcohol offenses and refusal to test
questions.text: A remote pilot employed by a Part 107 operator subject to DOT drug testing refuses to comply with a random drug test as directed. The operator reports the refusal to the FAA. Under 14 CFR Part 107, which consequence may the FAA impose for a drug test refusal?

answers.text: A mandatory 30-day administrative suspension from all sUAS operations pending a compliance review
Denial of an application for or revocation of any airman certificate held by the individual
A 90-day certificate suspension conditioned on submission of a clean drug test result within that window
A requirement to complete an FAA-approved substance abuse treatment program before resuming any sUAS operations

explanations.a: Administrative suspension from operations is not an FAA enforcement remedy; the FAA's authority is over certificates, not employment arrangements or work schedules.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.59, the FAA may deny an application for or revoke any airman certificate held by a person who refuses to submit to a drug or alcohol test required under applicable regulations.
explanations.c: A 90-day conditional suspension is not the Part 107 regulatory consequence; refusal can result in outright certificate denial or revocation, not a suspension contingent on a clean test.
explanations.d: While substance abuse programs may be recommended as part of a return-to-duty process, Part 107 specifies certificate denial or revocation for refusal, not mandatory program enrollment as a standalone regulatory remedy.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.19 Waiver policy and certificates of waiver
questions.text: A precision agriculture company wants its remote pilots to fly sUAS Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) to survey large fields more efficiently. No visual observer network is planned. Under 14 CFR Part 107, BVLOS operations require what regulatory action?

answers.text: A chain of visual observers spaced every half-mile along the flight path to collectively maintain VLOS coverage
A Part 107 Certificate of Waiver approved by the FAA that specifically authorizes BVLOS flight
Operating exclusively in Class G airspace below 200 ft AGL, which is automatically authorized for BVLOS flights
An experimental airworthiness certificate for the sUAS issued under 14 CFR Part 21 before any BVLOS flight

explanations.a: A chain of visual observers does not satisfy the BVLOS waiver requirement; each observer only covers their immediate area, and no networked VO arrangement substitutes for a formal waiver.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.200, an applicant may apply for a certificate of waiver from Part 107 operating rules, including the VLOS requirement; BVLOS operations require FAA approval through this waiver process.
explanations.c: There is no automatic BVLOS authorization at any altitude or in any airspace class; a waiver is required regardless of airspace classification.
explanations.d: Part 21 experimental certificates address aircraft airworthiness standards, not operational rule waivers; BVLOS authority flows from a Part 107 certificate of waiver.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.19 Waiver policy and certificates of waiver
questions.text: A remote pilot submits a Part 107 waiver application to conduct nighttime BVLOS operations using an FPV system and ground-based radar. The application must demonstrate what to receive FAA approval under 14 CFR 107.200?

answers.text: That the proposed operation can be safely conducted under the terms, conditions, and limitations of the certificate of waiver
That the remote pilot has accumulated a minimum of 200 logged sUAS flight hours in the 12 months preceding the application
That the sUAS has been issued an airworthiness certificate under 14 CFR Part 21 specific to the waived operation type
That both the FAA and the Department of Defense have independently reviewed and concurred with the proposed waiver terms

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.200, the FAA may issue a certificate of waiver if the proposed operation can be safely conducted under the terms, conditions, and limitations specified in the waiver; this safety demonstration is the central standard.
explanations.b: Flight hour minimums are not a universal prerequisite for Part 107 waivers; the demonstrated safety of the proposed operation is the applicable standard.
explanations.c: A Part 21 airworthiness certificate is not a requirement for Part 107 waiver approval; standard Part 107 aircraft are not type-certificated under Part 21.
explanations.d: DOD review is not part of the Part 107 waiver approval process; the FAA alone evaluates and issues certificates of waiver.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.14 Operating limitations
questions.text: A remote pilot is hired to inspect communications equipment on a 450-foot broadcast tower. The pilot positions the sUAS adjacent to the tower structure to conduct the inspection. Under 14 CFR Part 107, how high may the sUAS legally operate during this tower inspection without a waiver?

answers.text: 400 ft AGL maximum because the structure exception does not apply to broadcast towers under Part 107
500 ft AGL because the FAA grants a blanket 100-foot additional buffer for infrastructure inspection operations
Only up to the top of the structure at 450 ft AGL, because sUAS may not exceed the structure's own height
Up to 850 ft AGL, because the sUAS may fly up to 400 feet above the top of the 450-foot tower while within 400 feet of it

explanations.a: The structure exception explicitly applies to towers and similar vertical structures; the 400-ft-above-structure provision was designed for exactly this category of inspection work.
explanations.b: There is no blanket 100-foot infrastructure inspection buffer in Part 107; the correct structure exception allows 400 feet above the top of the structure.
explanations.c: Part 107 allows the sUAS to operate above the structure's top by up to 400 feet, not merely up to the height of the structure itself.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 107.51(b), when an sUAS is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure, it may operate up to 400 feet above the structure's uppermost point; for a 450-foot tower, this permits flight up to 850 ft AGL.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.7 Hazardous operations, alcohol/drugs
questions.text: A commercial videographer deliberately flies an sUAS within 10 feet of 200 festival spectators to capture dramatic close-up footage. Audience members duck and scatter to avoid the aircraft. No physical contact or injuries occur. The pilot argues no violation happened because no one was hurt. Under 14 CFR Part 107, how should this be classified?

answers.text: Permitted commercial activity because VLOS was maintained throughout and no physical injury resulted from the operation
A technical deviation excusable under an implied creative expression exception for licensed commercial media operations
Careless or reckless operation that endangered persons on the surface, regardless of whether physical contact occurred
Acceptable operation within Category 3 operations-over-people limits because no enclosed-structure requirement was violated

explanations.a: The absence of physical injury does not make a hazardous maneuver legal; Part 107 prohibits endangering persons, not merely causing physical harm.
explanations.b: There is no creative expression exception in Part 107 that excuses careless or reckless flying over crowds.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.23(a), no person may operate an sUAS in a careless or reckless manner so as to endanger the life or property of another; flying within 10 feet of a crowd and causing people to take evasive action constitutes endangerment regardless of physical contact.
explanations.d: Category 3 operations over people require a Declaration of Compliance and specific airworthiness criteria; they do not authorize flying within 10 feet of an open uncontrolled crowd of 200 people.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.6 Remote PIC responsibility, manipulating controls, in-flight emergency deviation
questions.text: A remote pilot is asked whether they can transfer remote PIC responsibilities to an experienced visual observer during a complex inspection flight so the pilot can focus on reviewing real-time payload imagery. Under 14 CFR Part 107, is such a transfer of PIC responsibility permitted?

answers.text: Yes, the visual observer may assume PIC duties during data-review segments when the remote pilot is focused on payload analysis
Yes, if the visual observer holds a current remote pilot certificate and the transfer is acknowledged in writing before the flight
Yes, but only for flights where the remote pilot must simultaneously operate additional specialized ground equipment
No, the remote PIC's responsibility and authority under Part 107 cannot be delegated to any other person

explanations.a: Visual observers perform a VLOS function and have no authority to assume PIC duties; responsibility remains with the certificated remote pilot at all times.
explanations.b: Even a certificated remote pilot serving as a visual observer cannot receive PIC responsibility through an informal transfer; Part 107 does not allow such delegation.
explanations.c: Pilot workload considerations do not create an exception to the non-delegable nature of PIC responsibility under Part 107.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 107.19, the remote PIC is responsible for the safe operation of the sUAS and this responsibility cannot be delegated; the remote pilot remains accountable for the entire flight.

questions.name: Regulations — Core
questions.objective: 1.12 Airspace authorization, operations near airports, prohibited/restricted areas, NOTAM-based TFRs
questions.keyword: Class G near non-towered airport no authorization
questions.text: A remote pilot plans to fly at 200 ft AGL approximately 2 miles from a non-towered general aviation airport. Before the flight, the pilot checks the sectional chart and confirms the area directly above the operation is Class G airspace up to 700 ft AGL. Under current Part 107 rules, what authorization is required for this specific flight?

answers.text: Written notification must be sent to both the airport manager and FAA Flight Service at least 24 hours before the flight
A NOTAM must be filed through FAA Flight Service at least 48 hours before the intended operation
No airspace authorization is required because the operation is entirely within Class G airspace, where sUAS may operate without ATC approval
Automatic LAANC approval is granted for all operations within 5 miles of any airport regardless of the airspace classification overhead

explanations.a: Part 107's old 5-mile airport notification provision has been superseded by the airspace class-based authorization system; notification alone is not the regulatory mechanism.
explanations.b: Filing a NOTAM does not substitute for or satisfy airspace authorization requirements; in Class G airspace, no authorization is needed at all.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.41, ATC authorization is required only for Class B, C, D, and surface Class E airspace; a confirmed Class G operation at 200 ft AGL may proceed without any ATC authorization, regardless of airport proximity.
explanations.d: LAANC is a tool for obtaining ATC authorization in controlled airspace; it does not automatically authorize operations in Class G, and airport proximity alone does not trigger a LAANC requirement.
